1:
Gill settles the speaker in a line: these are the prophet's own words, and he notes that the Targum introduces them so. Keil and Delitzsch place the verse structurally, as the opening of the answer God returns to the lamentation of the previous chapter, and summarise what is coming — a command to write the oracle plainly because it is certain but not immediate, then the word that the just shall live by his faith while the proud shall not continue, then a fivefold woe on the Chaldean who gathers all nations to himself with insatiable greed. Clarke gives the same map with a different emphasis, that the time fixed in the divine counsel for the destruction of the Jewish polity is awfully near, and that the vision was to be written legibly so that those who read it with attention might flee the impending vengeance. Wesley reduces the image to its plainest terms: a watchman on his watchtower, waiting on the Lord.

What the tower is divides them. Calvin refuses to let it stand for the prophetic office, disapproving of the interpreters who confine the verse that way, since the man speaks throughout in the person of the whole Church and not out of private feeling. For him the tower is patience arising from hope, and more exactly the recess of the mind into which we withdraw from the world; he allows in some measure the reading that makes it the Word of God, but thinks it not suitable in every respect. His reason is practical — left to our own inclination we cannot exercise hope for a moment, temptations lay hold of us at once, and Satan entangles men who wander among their own imaginations. Henry reads the tower as prudence rather than retreat, the use of every help within reach: those who expect to hear from God must get above the world, fix their thought, study the scriptures, consult experience and the experienced, and continue instant in prayer.

Ellicott traces the figure to the ordinary practice of climbing a height for an extensive view, and warns against pressing it into biography. We need not suppose the prophet literally betook himself to a solitary summit; Balaam the heathen soothsayer did so, but the conduct of a soothsayer throws no light on the customs of the Jewish prophets. Henry, who is willing to keep the picture concrete, has him standing like a sentinel on the walls of a besieged city or on the borders of an invaded country, anxious for intelligence, looking up and round and within, and he reads the standing on watch as constancy: the man will wait the time and weather the point, but he will have an answer.

The last clause divides them twice over. On what is heard, Ellicott corrects the received rendering to what He will say in me, so that the question is of what solution to the perplexities the prophet shall be made the mouthpiece; Keil and Delitzsch render it the same way, and Henry allows the reading and glosses it as what the Spirit of prophecy within will dictate, adding that God speaks in us by conscience as well as to us by his word. On what is answered they part. Wesley takes the reproof as a summons to give account of the mysteriousness of providence, either to satisfy doubters or to silence quarrellers, and Henry likewise has the prophet equipped to answer the exceptions of others; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch make the answer one returned to his own complaint, not to any opponent.
2:
Gill takes the answer as a pattern: God answers his ministers and people sooner or later, in one way or another, when they call on him with humility and reverence, with faith and fervency. Calvin makes the same generalisation the point of the verse. The prophet accommodates his own example to the common instruction of the whole Church, so that in testifying that an answer was given he means us to entertain a cheerful hope that the Lord, finding us stationed at our watchtower, will convey in due season the consolation he sees we need; and the command to write proves the truth was common property, since it was not for the writer's own sake but for the edification of all. Keil and Delitzsch mark the same place as the point where the prophecy itself commences, with the fundamental thought that the presumptuous will not continue and the just alone will live.

The tables and the running reader produce the sharpest disagreement in the chapter. Calvin says the letters were to be large, so that anyone passing by quickly might see at a glance what was written, and that the writing should not cause the readers to stop; the tablets he takes for wood or stone made smooth, noting that the Septuagint renders the word a plank of boxwood. Wesley agrees, and adds the custom: what was of public concern was anciently engraved on tables, smooth stones or wood and hung up in a public place, so that none should need to stop. Ellicott renders it that the reader may run his eye quickly through the prophecy, and observes that the definite article probably points to certain well-known tables on which prophets inscribed their utterances, though interpreters divide over whether these hung in the Temple or the market-place.

Clarke rejects that whole line and says so with unusual heat. The words do not mean that the writing is to be plain enough for a man running by to catch its sense; that interpretation has been given often and has been carelessly extended to the whole of Scripture in the saying that God's book is so plain that he who runs may read, and it is very foolish, since God never intends his words to be understood by the careless. Whoever reads, studies, meditates and prays will understand every part that bears on his own salvation, but no trifler will understand it; and Clarke adds that if a play-bill were read as many read the Bible, its readers would know as much of the one as they do of the other. His own reading of the clause is that the man who peruses the writing attentively may speed away and save his life from the coming irruption.

On the delay they are nearer together. Clarke observes that the destroyers must finish their work before they receive their wages, so that a term is fixed, and counsels against impatience since it will not tarry beyond the appointed time. Calvin draws the lesson that we must not deal with God in too limited a manner but leave room for hope, since he does not execute immediately what he declares, his purpose being to prove our patience and the obedience of our faith. Wesley reads the speaking at the end as accomplishment that will not disappoint expectation. Gill extends the promise beyond this oracle to prophecy in general, answering the fear that vision would cease with the captivity: prophets were given during it and after it. Ellicott calls the received rendering unfortunate, since the prophet has just said the vision will tarry, and prefers that it shall not be behindhand on its appointed day, the vision panting for the end that will do it justice.
4:
Ellicott renders the first clause that the soul within him is puffed up and not upright, and reads the inflation as self-dependence ousting every thought of God from the invader's mind, so that the soul is unsound and distorted; the inference that it must therefore die is left to be imagined while the prophet hastens to the antithesis. Clarke generalises it into a rule: whoever presumes on his own safety without a special warrant from God is a proud man, and whatever he professes or thinks of himself his mind is not upright in him. Wesley sharpens the same thought into two counts, that the man proudly contests with the justice and wisdom of divine providence and that he provides for his own safety by his own wit.

Calvin takes the clause a different way, and is explicit that he is choosing between readings. Others make it mean that the unbelieving, obstinate and perverted, are forever casting about for a place of safety, full of suspicions and resorting to the world for remedies against danger. Calvin prefers to hear a sentence pronounced: where there is elation of mind there is no tranquillity. On this reading the punishment such men have deserved is that they should always torment themselves, being their own executioners, seeking out troubles and sorrows and anxieties, mingling designs and purposes, thinking now of one thing and turning to another. He grounds it in usage — a soul is said to be right when it acquiesces and continues in a tranquil state, and not right when confused thoughts distract it — and he claims the doctrine so drawn is the more fruitful, since it can be verified in daily life: the man who fortifies himself and swells with self-confidence never finds a quiet haven, because some new suspicion or fear always disturbs him.

Gill hears the whole verse as describing two sorts of men differently affected toward the Messiah and the promise of his coming. The first clause points at the incredulous, those who disbelieved that coming and scoffed at the promise of it, and those who did not believe when he came although he bore every mark of the office. He identifies them with the proud Scribes and Pharisees, whose hearts he compares to bubbles blown up and full of wind, swelled with a high conceit of their own merit and holiness, disdaining those they thought beneath them and trusting to their own righteousness to the neglect of the righteousness offered them. He adds a philological observation, that the word rendered lifted up carries in it the sense of a hill, a mountain, a fortress or a tower.

The famous second clause divides them most of all. Ellicott cautions the student against the renderings he that is righteous by faith shall live and he that is justified by faith shall live, which the apostolic citations have suggested, holding that the adjective cannot be taken in that close collocation, and concluding that here at least the words carry no doctrinal significance, though their ethical importance is undeniable; for him the emphatic word is live, and the reward promised to patient waiting is deliverance from destruction. Clarke keeps the historical sense first — the man who believed what God said of the Chaldeans escaped the place and saved his life — and treats the later use as an accommodation, noting that the Christians who credited the warning about the city withdrew to Pella and lived while the unbelieving perished or were enslaved. Calvin sets faith against every defence by which men blind themselves into neglecting God: he who finds himself stripped of all protections will live by his faith, provided he seeks in God alone what he lacks. Wesley makes it the humble man persuaded of the truth of the promises, supporting himself by a firm expectation of deliverance.
5:
The particle that opens the verse is worked over carefully. Keil and Delitzsch deny that it can mean really if, insisting it always means still further or yea also that, taking on different force by context — to say nothing of the fact that, or all the more because — and here adding a new charge, that wine is treacherous to those addicted to it. Ellicott renders the whole in that key: add, too, that wine is treacherous, and that he is a braggart who cannot be quiet, whose appetite is large as that of Hades; so two more counts are laid beside the arrogance already charged, drunkenness and insatiable covetousness. Gill takes the particle as an argument from the lesser to the greater instead, reading it how much less or how much more: if a man elated with his own works of righteousness is not right within, how much less a drunken and ambitious heathen.

Whom the charge describes is disputed. Clarke names Nebuchadnezzar, proud and ambitious and inebriated with his successes. Henry calls the passage the burden of Babylon and Babylon's king, and is content to leave the doom hanging over Nebuchadnezzar, or the monarchy, or the whole Chaldean kingdom, or any proud and oppressive power that bears hard upon a people, while adding that the prophecy had its particular accomplishment in Belshazzar. Calvin widens it deliberately, judging that the words take in not the king only but the tyrannical empire with its people, whom he represents as a great company of robbers. Gill dissents from all of them. He denies that the Babylonian monarchs are meant at all, holding that to read the passage of the Chaldeans is to go back to times before the first coming of the Messiah and so to break the thread of a prophecy which carries the account of the enemies of Christ and his kingdom from that coming to the second.

On the wine itself Henry is the fullest. Drunkenness is a transgression in itself and the cause of an abundance of further transgression, and he presses the historical instance: the king was at the height of his transgression by wine when the writing on the wall signed the warrant for his immediate execution. Ellicott hears the clause as a kind of settled proverb, that it is a known fact wine is treacherous, and suspects the aphorism that wine is a mocker stands behind it. Clarke finds the received translation yields neither reason nor meaning in its first clause, and sets two other renderings beside it, one making the man transgress through wine as a mighty man does and so remain without rest, the other making him a despiser, powerful and proud, who yet shall have no rest.

The appetite draws the strongest images. Ellicott traces the figure to the insatiable appetite of death and the grave, twice described in the same wisdom book he has already cited. Clarke says that like the grave the man can never have enough: when he has obtained everything within reach he wishes for more, and becomes miserable because any limit at all is opposed to his ambition. He quotes the satirist on Alexander, that one world did not suffice the youth of Pella,, and adds the jest that the poet was right, since at the last the sarcophagus proved too large for his body. Calvin turns it back to the doctrine: though the Babylonians hurried here and there like drunken men under no control, the vengeance that would bring them to nothing was near, and all that follows to the end of the chapter serves to confirm that the just shall live by faith, of which no one can be convinced who does not first hold that God cares for us and governs the whole world.
6:
Keil and Delitzsch use the verse to lay out the architecture of everything that follows: from here to the end of the chapter the destruction already intimated is announced as a song of threatening sentences, five woes in five strophes of three verses each — on rapacity and plunder, on the attempt to establish a dynasty by force and cunning, on wicked ways of building, on the base treatment of subjugated nations, and on idolatry. Gill describes the form rather than the plan, calling the parable a proverbial expression, a laconic speech delivered in few words which yet contains much concerning the vices of the oppressor and imprecates judgment on him. Clarke supplies specimens of the kind of saying he means: he who towered so high, behold how low he is fallen; he made himself a god, and behold he herds with the beasts of the field; the disturber of the peace of the world is now a handful of dust.

The taunt's second clause divides the philologists. Ellicott rejects the familiar rendering outright: the man does not lade himself with thick clay but accumulates usury to himself, as the Targum has it, and the received translation rests on a false etymology which the student may find in the rabbinic commentary, the true derivation being available in the lexicons. Keil and Delitzsch keep the older rendering in their text without arguing for it. Ellicott presses the same commercial sense into the next verse: the verb rendered bite also means to oppress with usury and has that force here, so that the sentence is that the oppressor's turn will come and men will exact usury from him, while the verb rendered vex means literally to shake violently, in allusion to a creditor seizing his debtor by force.

Calvin will not have it. He grants that one translator renders the clause of those that have lent on usury, and calls it simply incorrect, partly because the corresponding word stands in the following line rather than the preceding one. The two answering words, he says, are biters and tormentors; the common meaning of the verb is to bite, and it carries the sense of lending on usury only in one conjugation, so the idea of usury cannot be admitted here — and he notes that the Septuagint gives biters. Gill sits between them, reporting the rendering thy usurers or thy creditors as something some give, without making it his own.

Who does the biting is a further division. Clarke and Ellicott both find the fulfilment in the Persians, Clarke with the detail that the troops entered Babylon through the bed of the river whose waters they had diverted into another channel, so that the inhabitants knew nothing of the matter until they saw the soldiers rise up as in a moment in the heart of their own city, and Ellicott dating the capture by the forces of Cyrus. Gill again carries the prophecy forward past the Persians altogether. For him the spoiled creditors are the Christians whose goods and substance had been plundered, and the sudden risers are the Christian emperors who overthrew the heathen ones, took away their power and wealth, and repaid the plundered with great gain. Calvin keeps the reference general, treating the words as the common taunts raised against the king of Babylon and the whole tyrannical empire by the many nations it had cruelly oppressed.
8:
Calvin states the ground of the sentence plainly: the passage shows why the Babylonians were to be dealt with so severely, since it would be a just reward that men who had given themselves to plunder, violence and cruelty should be plundered in their turn. God cannot be thought to treat them cruelly by inflicting so severe a punishment on those who had used so much inhumanity toward everyone else. He then draws the doctrinal use he draws everywhere in this chapter: when things in the world are in confusion we despond and hope vanishes, unless it comes to mind that as God is the judge of the world all the wicked must at length appear before his tribunal and account for their deeds, which is why Scripture sets God before us as a judge whenever the purpose is to allay our troubles.

Clarke and Ellicott both read the violence of the land as violence wreaked upon it rather than by it, Clarke naming the land of Judea and the city, and Ellicott noting that the same construction governs the parallel charge later in the chapter. Gill takes the remnant that spoils the spoiler in his own historical key: those who survived the persecutions of the emperors, the residue left of the great numbers put to death, rose up under Constantine and stripped the persecutors of all their power and wealth by just retaliation.

The second woe turns on building a house that cannot be reached. Ellicott renders it woe to him who accumulates wicked gain for his house and sets his nest on high to save himself from the hand of evil, and explains it as gathering spoil from the nations and stowing it in an impregnable treasure-house. He finds more than sufficient illustration for the nest set on high in the ancient accounts of Babylon, one historian giving the walls a height of three hundred and thirty-seven and a half feet and another three hundred, with towers of four hundred and twenty feet, two hundred and fifty of them irregularly disposed to guard the weaker stretches, and an enclosed space of about two hundred square miles. He also hears behind the language an earlier prophet's rebuke of a king of Judah, with the difference that there the sentence falls on individual sin.

Clarke keeps the reference dynastic: the king wished to aggrandise his family and make his empire permanent, and both family and empire were cut off with the death of his son and the fall of the Chaldean power. Wesley glosses the two phrases briefly, the house being the family he would enrich and raise high, and the deliverance being to keep himself secure and out of danger from everyone below him. Calvin insists the taunts are not scurrilous jests but serious threatenings, and that though the prophet puts the words in the mouth of the common people, in that multitude we are to recognise the innumerable heralds of God's vengeance; he also notices that the evil in the clause may be referred to the house itself, so that the sense is that a man who meant to provide for his household by heaping up riches will find the heap ruinous to it. Gill leaves the Chaldeans entirely and applies the covetousness to the bishops of Rome, enriched by imperial donation and still not satisfied, the greedy dogs of the older prophecy that could never have enough, gaping after more for themselves and their families and for a house which from the time of their apostasy stood over against the true house of God.
10:
Calvin reads the shame consulted for the house as an exact reversal of the builder's intention. The avaricious mean to prepare splendour for their posterity and to make their line illustrious by wealth, since it is commonly reckoned that the richer a man is the more he excels in dignity and the more he is to be esteemed; the prophet reminds them that they are greatly deceived, for the Lord will not merely frustrate their hopes but will turn the very thing they counted their glory into disgrace. Keil and Delitzsch put the same charge in the terms of the text, that the shame was consulted by cutting off many people, and connect it to the dynastic ambition of the previous woe. Clarke reduces the last clause to a sentence of forfeiture — thy life is forfeited by thy crimes — while Ellicott renders it more literally as sinning in thy soul, and takes it to mean that all the while the oppressor was plundering these peoples he was involving his soul in guilt.

Gill keeps the woe on the church he has been describing, and finds the shame in the outcome rather than the sentence: covetousness, ambition and arrogance brought a body that should have gained honour into disgrace with all good men, and did so as effectually as if the disgrace had been the thing studied and aimed at from the start.

The crying stone draws out a good deal. Clarke takes it as an architectural observation, referring the pairing of stone and beam to the ancient mode of walling in which two or three courses of stone were followed by a course of timber, the manner in which a famous palace was built; and since the celebrated buildings of Babylon were raised out of the spoils of conquered nations and at the expense of a multitude of lives, the stones and the timber are represented as calling out for vengeance. Ellicott says the same more starkly, that every stone in those giant walls reared by the enforced labour of captives cries aloud to accuse, and every spar out of the woodwork attests the charge. Wesley keeps the figure simple: the stone cries to God for vengeance as if it had a voice, and the beam confirms the accusation.

Calvin is interested in the device itself. He calls it a new personification, distinct from the taunt-song already composed for the mouths of all: speech is now ascribed to the stone and the wood of which buildings are made, so that no part of the structure will fail to cry out that it was raised by plunder and cruelty and evil deeds. What strikes him is that the materials are made to answer one another as in a chorus, in the way that voices in lyric poetry take up the song by turns. He notes too that the word rendered wood occurs nowhere else, and that the versions have guessed at it variously, though the context requires something belonging to timber construction. Gill, as before, reads the personification historically: the stones that cry are men from within the corrupted body itself who truly feared God and, seeing the covetousness and ambition and the anathemas, cried out against them in their sermons and their writings — and he names Bernard, Wycliffe and Huss among them.
12:
Gill and Clarke both take the woe as the speech of the building materials themselves — Gill saying this is what the stone and the beam would say if everyone else were silent, Clarke calling it the answer the beam returns to the stone. They then go different ways entirely. Gill identifies the town with the church of Rome, mystical Babylon called spiritually Egypt and Sodom, and its builders with the bishops in succession, tracing the title of head of the church to a grant from the murderer of an emperor, the foundation to the blood of saints shed in persecutions and wars, and the establishment to unjust exactions of tribute from subject countries and to the indulgences and processions by which money was extorted to support its pomp. Clarke turns instead to his own century and the slave trade, saying that the fortunes gained and the buildings erected by it show walls which, to a considerate and humane mind, appear composed of the bones of Africans and cemented by their blood — houses that soon come to ruin, and fortunes that have mostly become chaff before the whirlwind of God's indignation.

Calvin refuses to separate the blood from the iniquity, treating the two words as one charge. The avaricious may not kill innocent men outright, but they suck their blood, which is to kill by degrees through a slow tormenting process; and it is easier to undergo death at once than to pine away in want, as helpless men do when they are spoiled of all their property. Wherever there is wanton plundering there is murder committed in the sight of God, since a man who does not spare the helpless but drinks up their substance sins no less than if he had killed them outright.

He also explains why the prophet needed the device of speaking stones at all. We all confess that God judges the world, and nobody waits for his sentence before condemning avarice and cruelty, the very name of avarice being infamous and hated; and yet when we actually see the avaricious in splendour and esteem we are astounded, and no one is able to foresee by faith what is here declared. Because our dullness is so great, Calvin says — or rather our sottishness — it is no wonder the prophet should set the stones and the timber before us to say it.

Keil and Delitzsch identify the third woe as falling on the building of cities with the blood and property of strangers, and gloss the means as murder, bloodshed, transportation and tyranny of every kind. On the labour that comes to nothing, Ellicott points out that the same preposition governs both clauses and means an equivalent in, so that the sense is carried by rendering it labour only for the fire and weary themselves all for nothing; he notes that the same expressions stand in another prophet's denunciation of Babylon, who adds that her broad walls shall be utterly broken and her high gates burned, and that both prophets are predicting that all this compulsory service shall prove fruitless. Clarke reads it as a plain forecast that the superb buildings would be burnt down, and Wesley as a judgment from God, men going through the most painful labour and receiving nothing for it. Gill, following the Targum, applies it to the judgments coming on the bloody city, which those who labour to prevent labour in vain.
14:
Calvin reads the promise against the darkness it was uttered in. God did not appear in his own majesty when the people were dragged into exile, the temple demolished and the city levelled, nor while the whole eastern region lay open to rapine; and when the Babylonians, following the Assyrians, were swallowing their neighbours one after another, no splendour of his was conspicuous anywhere. The sufferers had themselves gone mute, stupefied by misery, their mouths closed so that they could not bless him from the heart while he afflicted them so severely; and amid that universal confusion the profane concluded that events fall out by chance and that no providence governs anything. God was hidden then, and the verse announces that he will be known again. Ellicott builds the same contrast into the structure of the chapter: the sentence stands here over against the brief splendour of Babylon, whose palaces the enslaved nations raised only for fire to consume, whereas what is promised here will be published the world over and never effaced.

Ellicott also adjusts the preposition, preferring as concerns the knowledge to the received with the knowledge, and observes that an earlier prophet had already given the identical promise. Clarke calls the verse singular and important, and declines to choose among its senses, offering three that ascend. It may be referred first to Babylon, since divine power and providence were widely displayed in the ruin of that city and empire, in the humbling of its king and in the captivity and return of the people. It may be carried next to the days of the Messiah, when the land would be filled by his preaching and his disciples' with a true acquaintance with God, the entire scheme of salvation being then uncovered and explained. And it may reach further still to the spread of the gospel across the habitable globe, when the fullness of the Gentiles should come in and the Jews be gathered with them.

Clarke states that third sense as a principle rather than a hope, holding that the world cannot perish until every continent, every island and every inhabitant has been lit by the gospel. Gill takes the promise christologically from the outset, without any graduated scheme. What fills the earth is for him the excellence of Christ, and he divides it in two. There is what belongs to his person as the Son of God and truly God, essential to him and underived, identical with his Father's and transcending that of every created being; and there is what belongs to his office as mediator, seen in his fitness for it, his faithful discharge of it and the honour given him upon it, as well as in the fullness of grace that makes him lovely to his people.

Gill then turns the prediction into a description of how such acquaintance actually shows itself, which is by the exercise of faith rather than by information held. Those filled with it honour Christ as the Lord their righteousness by resting on that righteousness and boasting in it, as their sole Saviour and Redeemer by looking to him and trusting him as such, as the one head of the church by cleaving to him, and as the only mediator between God and men by employing him for that purpose instead of resorting to angels or departed saints.
15:
Calvin thinks most expounders handle this verse frigidly, and says so before offering anything of his own. He is particularly hard on the Jewish interpreters, charging them with boldness in contriving fables whenever nothing certain occurs to them, and divining this or that without discrimination or shame. The specimen he has in view is the story that the Babylonian king was given to excess and drew everyone he could into the same vice, his associates being captive kings brought to his table for sport, whom he forced into intoxication by drinking their health so that he might laugh at them when they made themselves base and ridiculous. All of this Calvin calls groundless, on the plain ground that no history relates any such thing. His own conclusion is that the discourse is metaphorical or allegorical throughout, and that it is not aimed at a king only but at the whole empire.

Henry takes the opposite view and reads the woe literally, as an impeachment of the promoters of drunkenness. The king in whom he finds it verified is the one who drank wine before a thousand of his lords on the very night this chapter's prophecy was fulfilled in the ending of his life and kingdom, beginning the healths himself and forcing his company to pledge him; and Henry suggests that this example may be why the Persian monarchs who succeeded made it a law of the kingdom that in drinking none should compel, but every man should do according to his own pleasure. He also notes how closely the three preceding woes are related, all of them charging oppressors and extortioners who raise estates by rapine, and observes that the charge of innocent blood is repeated later in the chapter exactly as it stood earlier, because that is the count on which the greatest stress is laid.

Clarke looks for a particular historical culprit and finds one outside Babylon altogether. He reports the application of the verse to the Egyptian king who enticed his neighbours, the two last kings of Judah, into rebellion against the Chaldean power, with the result that the nakedness and imbecility of the poor Jews was soon discovered, since the Chaldeans quickly took the city and carried its kings, princes and people into captivity. On this reading the man who gives his neighbour drink is the ally who intoxicates a weaker state with false confidence and then leaves it exposed.

Gill agrees with Calvin that the sense is figurative and not literal, but applies the figure to a period neither of the others has in view. He places the practice after the Reformation and before the final destruction of the enemy, in the interval during which the promise of the earth being filled with the knowledge of the Lord has only had its fulfilment in part. Giving a neighbour drink he grants to be a commendable action in itself, when the drink is given to a man in want to quench his thirst or to one in distress to refresh and cheer him; it becomes an evil one when the purpose is to intoxicate him and draw him into uncleanness, which the woe pronounced and the clause that follows show to be the sense here. The artful and alluring methods he means are those he charges against the Jesuits in their dealings with Protestants, to make them forsake their religion.
16:
Clarke explains the cup from ancient table custom: all drank from the same vessel, which was passed from hand to hand while each took as much as he chose. On that footing the sentence is an exact retaliation — the Chaldeans handed the neighbouring nations the cup of idolatry and of deceitful alliance, and received in return from the Lord the cup of his fury. Wesley makes the same point in the same idiom, that those who turned the cup of pleasure about will find God carrying the cup of indignation about also and making them drink deep of it, and he presses the last clause without softening it: the man shall be as much loathed as a shameful drunkard is in his own vomit. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the structure, marking the point a little further on where the fifth and last strophe of the song begins with the question what a graven image profits its maker.

Gill reads the shame that comes instead of glory as the exact contrary of the promise two verses earlier. Where the earth was to be filled with the glory of the Lord and the knowledge of it, these are filled instead with shameful doctrines and abominable practices; and instead of seeking the glory of God and the honour of their neighbours they are satiated with the spectacle of an apostasy they themselves procured. What he finds worst is the absence of the shame the case calls for: rather than taking shame to themselves they glory in it, counting it an honour to have been the instruments of bringing others into uncleanness and idolatry, and glutting themselves on the sight.

Calvin uses the following verse as proof that his figurative reading of the drink was right. Here, he says, we may easily learn that the prophet has not been speaking of drunkenness at all, since what follows gives the reason for the punishment, and that reason is violence — exercised not against the nations indiscriminately only, but against the chosen people in particular. Having spoken generally of the cruelty by which the king of Babylon destroyed many nations, the prophet now speaks distinctly of the Jews, to show that God would be in a peculiar manner the avenger of the cruelty used toward them, because he had taken that people under his own protection and they had been adopted by him.

What the violence of Lebanon means divides the rest. Ellicott renders it the violence done to Lebanon shall overwhelm thee, together with the destruction of the beasts which it frightened away, and takes the beasts for cattle raided from the mountain's slopes; but he thinks more is included, and supposes the prophet foresees the invader felling the cedar forests to adorn the palaces of Babylon. He reports too that some commentators read it as a bold synecdoche in which Lebanon stands for the Holy Land, of which it was the beauty, or even for the Temple, both of which the conqueror laid waste. Clarke extends the violence to men, cattle, Judea and the city at once, and adds a possibility of his own, that this passage threatens Egypt as the earlier one threatened Chaldea. Wesley makes it simply the violence done to Judea, and reads the spoil of beasts as the kind of havoc hunters make when they set out to destroy a whole species.
18:
Calvin explains why the idols are brought in at all at this point. It would not have been enough, he says, to hold that some deity exists in heaven who rules human affairs so that tyrants must suffer for their cruelty, since sayings of that kind were common everywhere among the heathen — that justice sits beside Jupiter, that there is a Nemesis, that there is divine vengeance. A conviction so generally imprinted on men's hearts would have made the prophet's doctrine frigid and almost empty had he stopped there. So he introduces the God of Israel by name, derides all the idols, and claims the government of the whole world for him, showing plainly that he speaks as one of a people who worshipped no imaginary god but understood him to be the creator of heaven and earth, who had revealed himself to Abraham and given the law by the hand of Moses. Since the king of Babylon worshipped gods of his own, the point of the derision is to dissipate the vain confidence by which he was himself deceived and deceived others.

Clarke reads the verse more broadly still, as directed against idolatry in general and every species of it, and against the princes, priests and people who practise it and encourage others to do the same. He renders the last phrase dumb nothings, and observes that this agrees exactly with the apostle's statement that an idol is nothing in the world; then he presses the argument from history, asking what the idols worshipped by Chaldeans, Tyrians and Egyptians ever signified, since none of them proved able to save their worshippers.

Ellicott works on two phrases. The teacher of lies he takes to be not a false prophet but the idol itself, which points out false ways in opposition to God, the teacher of truth. The following clause he re-renders as that he who frames his image trusts in it, so as to make dumb idols; and he notices what Clarke's translation had already implied, that dumb nothings is perhaps the literal rendering of the Hebrew pair, whose words appear to have been chosen for their similarity of sound.

Gill applies the question to the images whose worship he charges against the church of Rome — of the Trinity, of Christ, of the Virgin, of angels and of departed saints, which he notes were still in use after the Reformation. He then answers the prophet's question with an accountant's exactness. The images may indeed be profitable to the graver, who is paid for graving them, and the metal or other material may turn to account if the thing is sold and converted to some other use; but considered as deities and worshipped as such they are of no profit whatever to their worshippers, since they cannot hear prayers or answer them, cannot bestow a favour or deliver out of any distress, and in particular cannot save anyone from the judgments already denounced in this chapter.
19:
Keil and Delitzsch render the woe without comment — a man saying to the wood awake and to the dumb stone arise, it shall teach, when the thing is laid over with gold and silver and there is no breath at all in the midst of it. Clarke draws the contrast that the rendering invites: it is foolish and contemptible to worship a thing formed by human hands out of wood or stone or gold, since the meanest brute is superior to them all, because it breathes and lives while they have no breath in them. He then resolves the difficulty left by the previous verse, which had called such images teachers of lies. They appeared to give out oracles, and the oracles were lies; but they were not given by the statue at all, and came from the priest.

Gill hears the address to the wood as a prayer, and takes it as covering two kinds of request equally: awake and exert thyself on our behalf, deliver us from present danger and save us from our enemies, but also pray and intercede for us that we may be delivered. He charges the second form as directly as the first, since to address a block of wood as one would address God himself, or as his people address him, must be displeasing and detestable to God, and it is on such worshippers that the woe is threatened.

Calvin explains why the true God is named only now, at the end, and insists the order is deliberate. It would not have been enough to strip the Babylonians of the false confidence they placed in their idols unless the people of God were on the other side fully persuaded that he was theirs and had taken them under his protection. He presses the point with an observation about his own day: many boldly deride every superstition in the world and at the same time despise the true God with a cyclopic fury, prating in jest against the errors of the papacy while under no fear of God whatever. If one of two evils must be chosen, Calvin judges superstition the more tolerable, for though the superstitious provoke God's wrath the more they toil in their delusions, transferring his glory to dead things, they at least retain the principle that honour and worship are due to God; whereas the profane not only change God from what he is but strive so far as they can to reduce him to nothing.

Where the holy temple is the voices divide. Gill puts it in heaven, the habitation of God's holiness, from which he surveys the actions of men, observes the stupidity of idol worshippers and answers the prayers of his own; or else in the church, which is his temple, where he grants his presence to those who worship in spirit and in truth. Ellicott locates it at Jerusalem, and reads the verse as the turn of the whole chapter: while all this false worship prevails the true ruler of the world abides, and the prophet, ceasing his denunciations of the invader, finds his solace in the ode that follows. Clarke stresses instead what is absent from it — Jehovah has a temple where he is worshipped, but there is no image there, and the oracles given from it are true and fulfilled in their season. For the silence commanded, Clarke offers a picture from the courts he knew, where the deepest silence reigns among viziers and ambassadors when the sovereign goes to worship. Wesley reads the command as a whole posture rather than a hush: fear, submit and depend on him, and wait for the one who will at last unfold the riddles of his providence.
